title: Git Stash and Worktrees: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on setting work aside with git stash (push, pop, apply, list, drop, untracked files, conflicts) and running parallel checkouts with git worktree, plus when to pick each.

chapters.title: Stash and Worktree Mental Model
points: Stash = a stack of commits (stash@{0} is newest) that saves tracked changes in the working tree and index, then resets the tree to HEAD
A stash entry is two or three commits: one for the working tree, one for the index, and an optional one for untracked files; it is local and never pushed
Worktree = an extra working directory linked to the same repository, with its own checked-out branch, HEAD and index
All worktrees share one .git object store and refs, so a commit made in one is instantly visible in the others
Rule of thumb: stash is for a short interruption you will return to in minutes; a worktree is for parallel work that lasts hours or days

chapters.title: Core Stash Workflow
points: git stash push -m "wip: login form" saves tracked changes with a label and cleans the tree; bare git stash is the same without a message
git stash list shows entries as stash@{0}, stash@{1}, ...; the newest is always index 0
git stash pop applies the newest stash and drops it only if the apply succeeded
git stash apply stash@{1} reapplies a chosen entry but keeps it on the stack, which makes it safe for applying the same stash to several branches
git stash drop stash@{n} deletes one entry; git stash clear deletes all of them

chapters.title: Everyday Stash Options
points: git stash push -u (--include-untracked) also stashes new untracked files; plain stash silently leaves them behind
git stash push -a (--all) also stashes ignored files, so use it rarely: it can sweep up build output and .env
git stash push -- path/to/file stashes only the listed paths (pathspec form)
git stash push -p picks hunks interactively, and --keep-index stashes while leaving staged changes in the working tree
git stash show -p stash@{0} prints the stash as a diff, and git stash branch fix/topic stash@{0} creates a branch from the commit where the stash was made, applies it, then drops it

chapters.title: Stash Conflicts and Safe Recovery
points: Pop or apply onto a changed base can conflict; resolve the files, then git add them (no commit is needed)
On a conflicted pop the stash is NOT dropped, so run git stash drop manually after you have resolved the conflict
git stash apply refuses to run when the working tree has local changes touching the same files; commit or stash first
A dropped stash can be recovered: git fsck --unreachable | grep commit finds the dangling commit, then git stash apply <sha>
git stash branch is the cleanest way out of persistent conflicts, because it replays the stash on the exact original base commit

chapters.title: Git Worktree Commands and Choosing Between Them
points: git worktree add ../hotfix -b fix/login creates a new directory with a new branch; git worktree add ../review origin/pr-branch checks out an existing ref
git worktree list shows each path, its HEAD commit and its branch; git worktree remove ../hotfix deletes a clean worktree (add --force if it is dirty)
One branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time, and git refuses a second checkout of the same branch
Deleting the folder by hand leaves stale metadata behind; clean it with git worktree prune
Choose a worktree to run long builds or tests while you keep coding, to review a PR without touching your work, or to hotfix mid-feature; choose stash for a quick context switch of a few minutes
Each worktree needs its own dependency install (node_modules, venv), because ignored files are not shared

chapters.title: Stash and Worktree Cheat Sheet
points: Stash: push -m "msg" | push -u | push -- path | push -p | list | show -p | apply | pop | drop | clear | branch name
Pop vs apply: pop = apply + drop on success; apply keeps the entry; a conflict keeps the entry in both cases
Worktree: add <path> -b <branch> | add <path> <ref> | list | remove <path> | prune
Pitfalls: untracked files need -u, a stash is not pushed, the same branch cannot be in two worktrees, a conflicted pop leaves the entry on the stack
Decision: minutes of interruption means stash; hours or parallel work means worktree; a stash you cannot finish means stash branch
